newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ asks China to explain apple smuggling attempt.
newsitem.headline: NZ asks China to explain apple smuggling attempt.

text.p: New Zealand has asked China for more information about a horticultural delegation that was intercepted trying to take a new strain of apple plants out of the country, officials said on Thursday.

In a combined police, customs and Ministry of Agriculture operation at Auckland airport last Sunday, 15 cuttings from a new apple variety developed by New Zealand researchers were found in the hand luggage of one of a group of five horticulturalists about to return to China.
They were given warnings but allowed to leave the country the following day after apologising, police said.
Customs Minister Neil Kirton told reporters he did not consider the allegations amounted to industrial espionage, and New Zealand would not prosecute any of the Chinese scientisits.

But with the fruit industry one of New Zealand's primary exporters, industry and opposition politicians have called for a tougher line. Both the foreign and commerce ministries said they were looking for more details.

"The incident is a very real concern," Associate Agriculture Minister John Luxton said in a statement. "Apparent attempts, such as this, to pirate the fruits of our research labours are very concerning."

Michael Green, divisional director for north Asia at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, told Reuters that New Zealand's ambassador to Beijing had "expressed our unhappiness over the incident" when he made an official complaint on Monday.
He had been promised a detailed response.
"They (Chinese officials) had no prior knowledge -- it was news to them. We're expecting them to return to us in due course," he said in a telephone interview.

Earlier Kirton, the minister in charge of enforcing export rules, sought to play down the incident, telling national radio: "We would expect at the other end they'll get their hands slapped -- I think that is the appropriate remedy."
Fruit farmers said they would be arguing strongly for stronger government action. Graham Jones, vice president of Fruit Growers of New Zealand, said his trade body saw no excuse for leniency.

"It's just not good enough as far as the New Zealand fruit growing industry is concerned -- we've got to make further representations to government and ensure that this sort of thing is not allowed to happen again," he said.
Leading opposition Labour Party MP and former prime minister Mike Moore said Kirton's "limp-wristed attitude will encourage our foreign competitors to come here and try again to steal our secrets".
"This is a major case of espionage and should be treated accordingly," he added.
New Zealand's horticultural exports rose in value by eight percent to nearly NZ$1.6 billion ($1.1 billion) in 1996, according to Commerce Ministry data.
